other_authors.author: bbolen83
other_authors.original: Published neural architectures and simulation software provide a foundation for this work \citep{rybak_modelling_2006, mccrea_organization_2008, markin_afferent_2010, nourse_sns_2023}. A circuit that coordinates the legs of a human model will produce a different movement when artificial muscles pull on a robot. Our first simulated walker ran slowly, and we tuned its controller by hand. I wanted to change either the controller or the mechanical model, hold the other fixed, and repeat the same experiment.
other_authors.proposed: The robot’s artificial muscles differ from human muscles in how much force they produce and where they pull on the skeleton. A circuit that coordinates the legs of the human model will therefore produce a different movement in the robot model, and that movement will change the sensory feedback the circuit receives. To measure the effect of the mechanics, I wanted to repeat the same experiment on both models with the controller held fixed. I also wanted to test changes to the controller while keeping the mechanical model fixed. Our first neuromechanical model ran slowly, and we tuned its controller by hand, making a series of these comparisons impractical.
